items.prompt: Which element must be present for a contract to be valid?

options.label: A written document of many pages
Value exchanged by both parties
A witness from a government office
A notary's stamp on the document

rubric: Consideration, meaning something of value exchanged, is a core element of a contract.
Distractors treat formalities such as notarisation, length or witnesses as always required.

items.prompt: Which business structure is owned by one person with no legal separation between the owner and the business?

options.label: Limited liability company
Sole proprietorship
Public limited company
Corporation

rubric: A sole proprietorship has no legal separation between owner and business.
The other structures are separate legal entities.

items.prompt: What does a trademark protect?

options.label: Brand names and logos that identify goods
Written works such as novels and manuals
Inventions that have a new technical function
Secret recipes kept confidential by the firm

rubric: Trademarks protect signs, names and logos that identify the source of goods or services.
Distractors describe patents, copyright and trade secrets.

items.prompt: What is a breach of contract?

options.label: Failing to perform a contract duty without legal excuse
Signing a contract without having read every one of its clauses
A change to the contract wording that both parties agree on in writing
Ending the contract early because both parties agree to end it

rubric: A breach is non-performance of a contractual obligation without a lawful excuse.
Distractors describe amendment, mutual termination and careless signing.

items.prompt: Which term names the legal rule that sets the lowest hourly pay an employer may offer?

options.label: Overtime premium
Performance bonus
Profit share
Minimum wage

rubric: Minimum wage is the legal floor for pay.
Other options are pay extras, not legal floors.

items.prompt: Which of the following are types of intellectual property? Select all that apply.

options.label: Patent
Trademark
Invoice
Payroll
Copyright

rubric: Patents, copyrights and trademarks are intellectual property rights.
Invoices and payroll are business records or processes, not IP.

items.prompt: A small company is sued and loses. The court orders it to pay damages, but the owners only risk losing what they invested in the company, not their homes. What is the name of this protection?

options.label: Joint liability
Strict liability
Vicarious liability
Limited liability

rubric: Limited liability caps owners' loss at their investment.
Distractors are other liability terms with different meanings.

items.prompt: Why does forming an LLC usually protect an owner's home from business debts?

options.label: The business is a separate legal entity that owes its own debts
State law makes the LLC's insurer pay debts the business cannot cover
Keeping business money in a separate bank account makes owners immune
Creditors usually cannot sue a business that is registered with the state

rubric: An LLC is a separate legal entity, so its debts belong to it rather than to the owners.
Distractors invent insurance, banking or immunity rules.

items.prompt: Why is it wise for a business to put important agreements in writing?

options.label: It stops either party from ever changing the terms later
It gives clear proof of the agreed terms if a dispute arises
It removes the need to perform the duties agreed later
It makes the contract legal, since oral contracts are never valid

rubric: Written terms serve as evidence in a dispute.
Distractors wrongly claim oral contracts are never valid or that writing removes duties or flexibility.

items.prompt: A company invents a new type of water filter. Which protection fits the invention itself?

options.label: Non-compete clause
Copyright
Trademark
Patent

rubric: Patents protect new inventions.
Copyright covers creative works, and trademarks cover brand identifiers.

items.prompt: Which worker is most likely to be treated as an independent contractor rather than an employee?

options.label: A clerk who is trained by the firm, uses its equipment daily and works set office hours
A designer who sets her hours, uses her own tools and has several clients
A cashier who follows a set schedule, is paid hourly and works only for one shop
A driver who must follow the firm's routes, wear its uniform and use its van

rubric: Control over hours and methods, own tools and multiple clients point to contractor status.
Distractors show employer control, which suggests employment.

items.prompt: A supplier promises in an email to give a shop 50 free display stands as a gift, and the shop promises nothing in return. If the supplier backs out, what is the most likely legal outcome?

options.label: The promise is void because email is not valid evidence of an agreement
The promise is enforceable because the shop relied on the email message
The promise is likely unenforceable because no value was exchanged
The promise is enforceable because it was put in writing by the supplier

rubric: A bare gift promise generally lacks consideration and so is not an enforceable contract.
Distractors assume writing or email alone creates a contract.

items.prompt: Which of these actions are examples of regulatory compliance for a business? Select all that apply.

options.label: Obtaining a licence needed for the trade
Writing a new advertising slogan
Filing required tax returns on time
Choosing a new logo colour
Keeping workplace safety records

rubric: Tax filings, licences and safety records are duties imposed by regulators.
Logo colour and slogans are branding choices, not compliance.

items.prompt: A supplier emails a cafe offering 100 mugs at $5 each, open until Friday. On Thursday the cafe replies, "We accept." On Friday the supplier says it has changed its mind and wants $7 each. What is the most likely legal position?

options.label: A contract exists only once the cafe has paid the full $500 price
A binding contract at $5 exists because the offer was accepted in time
The supplier may set a new price because the mugs have not been delivered
No contract exists because nothing was signed in ink by both parties

rubric: An offer accepted before it lapses forms a binding contract.
Distractors assume signatures, delivery or payment are needed to form a contract.

items.prompt: Which situation best shows a valid contract has been formed?

options.label: A client privately decides to hire a designer someday
A shop owner offers a price, and a customer accepts and pays
A friend says they might help move your office next week
A supplier emails a general price list to many different firms

rubric: A contract needs offer, acceptance and consideration; here all are present.
Price lists are usually invitations to treat, and vague intentions are not agreements.

items.prompt: Why do many small business owners choose a limited liability company (LLC) over operating as a sole proprietor?

options.label: It removes the need to follow any tax or filing rules
It lets the owner ignore contracts signed in the company name
It generally separates personal assets from business debts
It guarantees the business will never be sued by anyone

rubric: Limited liability protects owners' personal assets from most business debts.
Distractors overstate protection; LLCs still have filings, can be sued, and are bound by contracts.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a trademark for a business?

options.label: To protect the secret recipe used to make a product
To identify the source of goods or services for customers
To give exclusive rights over a new technical invention
To stop others from copying a written training manual

rubric: Trademarks protect brand identifiers like names and logos.
Other options describe trade secrets, patents and copyright.

items.prompt: Which best describes the difference between an employee and an independent contractor?

options.label: An employee works under the firm's control; a contractor controls how the work is done
An employee is paid through payroll with tax withheld; a contractor must be paid a higher rate
A contractor is the one who is entitled to a written contract; an employee works on verbal terms
An employee works set hours at the firm's premises; a contractor may do so only when unpaid

rubric: Control over how work is done is a key test of employment status.
Pay level, having a contract, and fixed hours are not the defining distinction.

items.prompt: What does 'breach of contract' mean?

options.label: A party reads the contract in full but still chooses to sign it anyway
A party fails to perform a promised duty with no legal excuse
A contract is signed by two parties who are in different cities
A party asks to renegotiate one term shortly before the deadline

rubric: Breach is non-performance of a contractual duty without lawful excuse.
Renegotiating or signing remotely is not a breach.

items.prompt: Which of the following are generally features of a general partnership? Select all that apply.

options.label: Partners can be personally liable for business debts
Profits are usually shared among the partners
It is a separate entity that fully shields owners' assets
Partners cannot act on behalf of the business

rubric: Partnerships typically share profits and expose partners to personal liability.
Distractors confuse partnerships with corporations and ignore partners' agency.

items.prompt: A bakery owner hires a freelance photographer to take product photos. Nothing is written down about who owns the pictures. Later the owner puts them on a website, and the photographer objects. Which principle best explains the dispute?

options.label: Copyright passes automatically once the photos are posted online
The creator usually owns copyright unless it is assigned in writing
Photos cannot be copyrighted when they are used for commercial purposes
The business that pays for the work owns the copyright unless the freelancer reserved it

rubric: Freelancers generally keep copyright unless a written assignment or licence exists.
Payment alone does not transfer copyright, and commercial use does not remove protection.

items.prompt: A café agrees by email to buy 100 mugs for $500. The supplier delivers on time, but the café refuses to pay, saying nothing was signed on paper. What is the most likely result?

options.label: The email agreement can still be an enforceable contract
The agreement is unenforceable because it lacked a handwritten signature
The agreement is unenforceable until a lawyer reviews and approves it
The agreement is unenforceable because the price was under a set legal minimum

rubric: Most ordinary contracts can be formed by email if the elements exist.
Paper signatures and lawyers are generally not required for such sales.

items.prompt: Maya runs a consulting firm as a sole proprietor and is sued for a $60,000 client loss. Her business has $5,000 in assets. What is the likely exposure?

options.label: Her clients become liable for the remaining amount
Only the $5,000 in business assets can be claimed by the court
The claim is dropped because she has no employees
Her personal assets may be reachable for the judgment

rubric: A sole proprietor has no separation between personal and business liability.
Limiting to business assets applies to entities like LLCs, not sole proprietorships.

items.prompt: A startup wants to stop competitors from using its new company name and logo on similar products. Which step best fits that goal?

options.label: Register the name and logo as trademarks
Sign a nondisclosure agreement with each customer
File a copyright on the company's tax records
Apply for a patent on the company's name

rubric: Trademark registration protects brand names and logos.
Patents cover inventions, copyright covers creative works, and NDAs protect confidential information.

items.prompt: A store owner wants to share a confidential customer pricing formula with a potential manufacturing partner before talks. Which tool best protects the information?

options.label: A signed nondisclosure agreement before sharing
A business licence displayed in the shop window
A verbal promise made at the start of the meeting
A trademark registration for the formula's name

rubric: An NDA creates enforceable confidentiality duties.
Trademarks and licences do not protect confidential information, and verbal promises are hard to prove.

items.prompt: A new restaurant owner is about to open. Which action best addresses regulatory compliance?

options.label: Obtain required local permits and health inspections first
Rely on the landlord to hold every permit the restaurant needs
Register the trademark, since it covers food safety law
Open first and apply for permits if a complaint arrives

rubric: Compliance means obtaining permits and inspections before operating.
Delaying, assuming others handle it, or confusing IP with safety rules is risky.

items.prompt: A small firm is about to hire its first employee. Which steps fit basic employment compliance? Select all that apply.

options.label: Confirm the worker's right to work as required locally
Pay at least the legal minimum wage
Skip payroll tax setup until the first audit
Treat the worker as a contractor to avoid obligations

rubric: Employers must verify work eligibility and meet minimum wage rules.
Delaying payroll tax and mislabelling employees as contractors create legal risk.

items.prompt: A landscaper is asked to sign a supplier contract containing an unfamiliar clause making her liable for unlimited damages. The deal is worth $2,000 a year. She is unsure what it means. What is the best action?

options.label: Sign now and ask a lawyer only if a dispute arises later
Cross out the clause and sign without telling the supplier
Sign it, since small deals never carry meaningful legal risk
Ask a lawyer to review the clause or negotiate it before signing

rubric: Unlimited liability is a significant risk worth review before signing.
Small deal size does not cap exposure, and secret edits or later review fail to manage the risk.

items.prompt: Mara emails a supplier: 'I'll buy 500 units at $10 each, delivery by June 1.' The supplier replies: 'Agreed at $10, but delivery will be June 15.' Applying the basic offer-and-acceptance rule, what is the legal status?

options.label: The reply is a counteroffer, so no contract exists until Mara accepts June 15
No contract can arise, because an email cannot carry an offer and acceptance
A binding contract exists with delivery on June 15, since the supplier replied
A binding contract exists at $10 with delivery on June 1, since price was agreed

rubric: Acceptance must match the offer's terms; a changed delivery date makes the reply a counteroffer.
Distractors assume agreement on price alone or that the reply automatically binds.

items.prompt: Two friends start a bakery together, sharing profits, and never file any paperwork. A supplier sues over an unpaid $20,000 invoice signed by one friend for the bakery. Which outcome is most likely under default rules?

options.label: Only the friend who signed is liable, since the other never saw or approved the invoice
The bakery alone is liable, since any business is treated as a separate legal person
Neither is liable, since no entity was ever registered with the state to take on debts
Both can be personally liable, since they form a general partnership by default

rubric: Co-owners sharing profits form a general partnership by default, with joint personal liability.
Distractors assume a separate entity exists without registration or that liability follows only the signer.

items.prompt: A freelance designer creates a logo for a client under a one-page agreement that says nothing about ownership. No employment relationship exists. Applying the usual default rule, who owns the copyright in the logo?

options.label: Both jointly, since each contributed to the final result
The client, because the logo carries the client's brand name
The designer, unless it is assigned in writing to the client
The client, once the agreed fee has been paid in full to the designer

rubric: An independent contractor generally keeps copyright unless there is a written assignment.
Distractors assume payment or use transfers ownership.

items.prompt: A café owner wants to offer a new employee unpaid trial shifts for two weeks, working normally with customers and receiving no wages. Applying basic employment rules, what is the best step?

options.label: Skip pay, since a short trial period is excluded from wage laws if it lasts under a month
Skip pay if the person verbally agrees, since informed consent waives the right to wages
Pay only tips, since customer-facing roles may use tips instead of wages for trial shifts
Pay at least minimum wage, since people doing real work are generally employees

rubric: Productive work in a business typically creates an employment relationship that requires wages.
Distractors rely on trial or consent exceptions that generally do not exist.

items.prompt: A small company wants to protect its unique product name 'BrightLeaf' for tea sold across the country. Which step best fits that goal?

options.label: File a patent on the name, since it identifies the invention
Register the name as a trademark for tea products
Incorporate the company, since that fully protects every product name
Register the copyright on the name, since it is original text

rubric: Trademarks protect brand names that identify goods.
Patents and copyrights cover inventions and creative works, and incorporation only reserves a company name.

items.prompt: Applying the basic elements of a valid contract, which of these situations contain an enforceable contract? Select all that apply.

options.label: A written deal to sell a used van for $4,000, signed by both adults
A promise to give a friend a gift next month, with nothing asked in return
A signed agreement for an illegal drug sale between two adults
A verbal agreement to paint an office for $800, then performed in full

rubric: Offer, acceptance, consideration and legality make a contract; a verbal service deal is generally enforceable.
A gratuitous promise lacks consideration and an illegal deal lacks lawful purpose.

items.prompt: Dev runs a landscaping company as a sole proprietor. He wants to limit personal exposure if a client is injured on a job and sues for $300,000. He has little cash but owns his home. He asks what to do before taking on bigger jobs. Which step best matches the aim?

options.label: Put the business bank account in his spouse's name only to hide assets
Form an LLC, keep its finances separate, and carry liability insurance
Register a trade name for the business, since that separates his home from business debts
Add a note on every invoice saying the business is not responsible for any client injuries

rubric: An LLC kept separate, plus insurance, limits personal exposure to business debts.
A trade name does not create a separate entity, and disclaimers or hiding assets are weak or improper.

items.prompt: A founder formed an LLC but pays personal bills from the company account, has no operating agreement, and leaves the LLC undercapitalised. A creditor sues her personally. Which analysis best explains why she may be liable?

options.label: A court may hold her liable mainly because she has no written operating agreement, which LLC statutes require for limited liability
A court may hold her liable because LLC protection covers only contract debts, so any creditor can reach her personally
A court may pierce the veil because she ignored the separation between herself and the LLC
A court may hold her liable because owners who lend no personal guarantee lose the shield once the LLC is sued

rubric: Commingling funds and undercapitalisation are classic factors for veil piercing.
Distractors treat liability shield as void by default or hinge on one missing document.

items.prompt: A buyer refuses to pay for custom software, claiming it is slow. The contract required delivery 'in good working order' and defined no speed standard. The seller says it works as specified in a signed spec sheet that lists features only. Which factor most affects who is likely to prevail?

options.label: Whether the software was delivered on time, since lateness alone settles quality claims
Whether the contract terms and spec sheet define performance, since vague terms invite dispute
Whether the buyer feels unhappy, since customer satisfaction decides all disputes
Whether the seller is larger, since bigger parties win ambiguous terms

rubric: Ambiguous terms make outcomes depend on what the documents actually specify.
Distractors replace the contract analysis with feelings, size or an unrelated factor.

items.prompt: A manager classifies a full-time delivery driver as an independent contractor, yet sets the driver's hours, routes and uniform, and supplies the van. Which feature most strongly suggests the classification is wrong?

options.label: The driver signed a contract labelled 'independent contractor agreement'
The company controls how, when and with what equipment the work is done
The driver works for the company in a single city only
The driver is paid per delivery rather than a monthly salary

rubric: Control over the manner of work is the central test of employment status.
Labels and pay method are not decisive, and location is irrelevant.

items.prompt: A startup's two founders each wrote code before incorporating. Later an investor's due diligence finds no written assignment of that code to the company, and one founder has left. Which risk does this most directly expose?

options.label: The company may not hold clear title to its core software
The investor automatically becomes owner of the departed founder's code
The code is placed in the public domain until assignments are signed
The company must pay corporate tax twice on the software's value

rubric: Without written assignment, authors may retain copyright, creating a chain-of-title gap.
Distractors invent tax, investor ownership or public domain consequences.

items.prompt: A shop owner is fined for selling a regulated product without a required licence. She says she did not know about the licence. Which analysis best describes the usual legal position?

options.label: Not knowing about a licensing rule is generally no defence, so the fine likely stands
The fine usually applies to large chains rather than small shops, which regulators treat leniently
The fine usually stands only if she had earlier received a written warning from the regulator
The fine is usually cancelled when the owner shows she honestly did not know the rule existed

rubric: Regulatory compliance is generally strict; not knowing the rule rarely excuses it.
Distractors invent a knowledge, warning or size exemption.

items.prompt: A client says a consultant's signed proposal is not binding because it was 'only a quote'. Which facts would help show a binding contract formed? Select all that apply.

options.label: The consultant privately hoped the client would hire the firm
The client signed and returned it, then asked the consultant to begin work
The proposal stated price, scope and dates, and said 'accept by signing'
The client later said, in passing, that the price felt a bit high

rubric: A definite offer with terms, followed by signed acceptance and conduct, supports formation.
Private hopes and passing comments do not show offer or acceptance.

items.prompt: A bakery owner hired a baker who signed a non-compete barring work at any bakery worldwide for ten years. The baker is dismissed and opens a stall across town. The owner wants a court order stopping her. Which analysis best predicts the outcome?

options.label: A court will void it, since any restriction on working after leaving a job is against public policy
A court will enforce it in full, because the baker signed voluntarily and a contract binds as written
A court will enforce it, because dismissal by the employer removes the baker's defences to the restriction
A court may refuse enforcement, since the scope and duration exceed what protects legitimate interests

rubric: Non-competes are generally enforced only if reasonable in scope, time and geography.
Distractors treat signature as decisive or assume blanket invalidity.

items.prompt: A seller emails a buyer: 'I'm thinking of selling my van for around $8,000. Interested?' The buyer replies: 'Yes, I accept.' Why is there most likely no binding contract yet?

options.label: Email acceptance is invalid unless the buyer follows up with a signed paper copy
The seller's message invited negotiation and did not show a definite intent to be bound
The buyer has not yet paid a deposit, and a contract needs money to change hands first
The price was approximate, and a price term must always be exact to the cent

rubric: The seller's message was an invitation to negotiate, not a firm offer that could be accepted.
Distractors wrongly require payment, paper signatures or exact figures as preconditions.

items.prompt: A buyer offers in writing to buy 200 chairs at $40 each, delivered on the 1st. The seller replies: 'Agreed at $40, but delivery on the 10th.' The buyer says nothing further. What is the legal position?

options.label: No contract yet: the reply was a counteroffer that ended the original offer, and silence is not acceptance
A contract exists on the seller's terms, because the buyer's silence shows consent to the new delivery date and the seller already agreed the price
A contract exists on the buyer's terms, because the delivery date is only a minor detail and the seller accepted the price and quantity
A contract exists on the original terms, because the seller accepted the price, which is the core term of any sale of goods

rubric: A reply that changes terms is a counteroffer and ends the original offer; silence does not accept it.
Distractors treat a changed term as minor or treat silence as consent.

items.prompt: A founder's LLC defaults on a bank loan and has no assets. The bank pursues the founder's house. The founder had signed a separate page in the loan papers. Which explanation best accounts for the personal exposure?

options.label: The founder signed a personal guarantee, which is a separate promise outside the LLC's shield
Banks can reach an owner's home when a single-member LLC lacks a separate bank account and an operating agreement
Limited liability usually covers tort claims but not contractual debts, so lenders may pursue owners for LLC loans
A court lifts the veil once an LLC is insolvent, since an entity unable to repay its lender loses protection

rubric: A personal guarantee is the founder's own contract, so the entity's limited liability does not protect against it.
Distractors misstate the scope of limited liability or assume automatic veil piercing.

items.prompt: In a dispute over whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor, which fact most strongly points toward employee status?

options.label: The worker signed an agreement titled 'independent contractor agreement' before starting work for the company
The company sets daily hours, dictates the methods used and supplies the tools
The worker is paid against invoices rather than through monthly payroll
The worker has performed the same type of task for the company for over a year

rubric: Control over when, how and with what the work is done is the strongest indicator of employment.
Labels, payment method and duration alone are weak indicators; substance outweighs form.

items.prompt: A café registers the company name 'Bean Lane Ltd'. A competitor in the same city later opens as 'Bean Lane Coffee'. The café assumes registration protects its name. Which analysis is most accurate?

options.label: Company registration mainly reserves the name on a register; trademark rights come from trade use or trademark registration
Company registration usually gives exclusive rights to the name for all goods and services, so the café can stop any similar name nationwide
Company registration usually gives protection in the café's own city, because local competitors are blocked by the register, though not elsewhere
Company registration works like a patent for a brand name, so protection lasts as long as annual filings are kept up to date

rubric: Company-name registration is administrative and does not by itself create trademark rights.
Distractors invent automatic nationwide rights, waiting periods or patent requirements.

items.prompt: A vendor made five statements while selling accounting software. Which are most likely treated as statements of fact that could support a misrepresentation claim, rather than sales puffery? Select all that apply.

options.label: The software reconciles bank feeds from the 12 banks listed on our website.
The product passed an independent security audit earlier this year.
Our software is simply the best on the market.
You will never regret choosing us.
Our clients simply love using it.

rubric: Specific, verifiable claims about features and audits are statements of fact that can be proved false.
Vague superlatives and enthusiasm are puffery that no reasonable buyer treats as a factual promise.

items.prompt: Mia and Raj run a design studio together, sharing profits, with no written agreement or registration. Without telling Raj, Mia signs a two-year lease in the studio's name. The studio fails and Mia disappears. The landlord sues. Which analysis best describes Raj's exposure?

options.label: Raj is protected, because an unregistered business is treated as having no legal obligations
Raj is likely jointly liable, because a partner can bind the firm in its usual business
Raj is not liable, because he never signed the lease or approved it himself
Raj is liable only for half the rent, because liability always follows the profit share

rubric: Partners in a general partnership generally bind each other and are jointly liable for acts within the usual course of business.
Distractors assume that lack of personal signature, profit share or registration limits liability.

items.prompt: Two founders plan a software startup, expect to raise venture capital within a year, will need to issue preferred shares, and want protection from product claims. Judged against these criteria, which structure fits best?

options.label: An unregistered joint venture, because investor terms and liability can be agreed between the founders later
A sole proprietorship for one founder, with the other engaged as an employee under a written contract
A corporation, because it gives a liability shield and the share structure investors expect
A general partnership, because it is quick to set up and profits are taxed once at partner level

rubric: A corporation offers limited liability and classes of shares that venture investors expect.
Distractors fail the liability or share-issuing criteria despite offering speed or simplicity.

items.prompt: A 10-person firm is buying payroll software. The vendor's draft caps all liability at one month's fees (about $400). The firm fears a data breach, but the vendor refuses unlimited liability. Which counter-proposal best balances the criteria?

options.label: Remove the cap and demand unlimited liability, since a vendor holding payroll data should carry all of the risk
Accept the one-month cap, since a court would likely set aside a cap this low as unreasonable
Keep the cap and add a clause that the vendor will use best efforts to prevent any data breach
A higher separate cap for data-breach losses, set as a multiple of annual fees and backed by insurance

rubric: A tiered cap for the specific high-risk loss is a realistic compromise that gives meaningful recovery.
Distractors rely on courts to rescue the firm, make an unrealistic demand, or add a toothless promise.

items.prompt: A 40-person firm has four compliance gaps. Ranking by likelihood of enforcement and size of financial exposure, which should be fixed first?

options.label: A staff handbook not reviewed for two years, with outdated policies that could weaken the firm's position in an employee dispute
Twelve full-time staff paid as contractors, risking back taxes, penalties and benefit claims
An annual report filed three weeks late, which carries a small fixed late fee but could lead to administrative strike-off if ignored
A secondary product name not registered as a trademark, so a competitor could register it and force a costly rebrand

rubric: Misclassification combines active enforcement by tax and labour authorities with large cumulative liabilities.
The other gaps carry low penalties or only speculative exposure.

items.prompt: On a tight budget, a founder asks when a lawyer is worth paying for rather than using a template. Judged by stakes and complexity, which task most clearly justifies a lawyer?

options.label: Renewing a one-year office-supplies order with the same supplier on last year's terms, with no price change
Updating the copyright year in the footer of the company website and the privacy page
Sending the firm's standard NDA template to a routine vendor for signature before a pricing call
Negotiating an investor term sheet with anti-dilution and drag-along rights

rubric: Equity financing terms are high-stakes, complex and hard to reverse, so professional advice pays off.
The other tasks are routine, low-value or standardised and are reasonable to handle with templates.

items.prompt: A manager says: 'The supplier only promised delivery by phone, so it isn't a binding contract and we can ignore it.' Which critique of this reasoning is soundest?

options.label: It is flawed: oral agreements can bind, proof of terms is the issue, and some types need writing
It is flawed only if the supplier already delivered part of the goods, since oral deals usually bind from then on
It is sound, because courts generally enforce agreements that both parties have signed on paper and not others
It is sound for a deal below a set value, because small oral deals are typically exempt from enforcement

rubric: Many oral contracts are enforceable; evidence is the practical problem, and only certain categories require writing.
Distractors assume a universal signed-writing rule, a part-performance precondition or a small-deal exemption.

items.prompt: Three co-founders want to reduce the risk that a dispute or an early departure destroys the company. Which provisions best meet that aim? Select all that apply.

options.label: A buy-sell clause setting how a departing founder's shares are valued and bought
A requirement that every decision be unanimous, with no tie-break mechanism
Vesting of each founder's shares over several years with a one-year cliff
A deadlock procedure such as mediation followed by a defined exit route
An oral understanding that equity will be adjusted fairly if anyone leaves

rubric: Vesting, buy-sell terms and deadlock procedures give predictable outcomes for departures and disputes.
Unanimity without a tie-break worsens deadlock, and oral understandings are hard to prove and vague.

items.prompt: A bakery named 'Crumb & Co' receives a letter from a national chain, 'Crumbco', demanding it stop using its name within 14 days. The bakery has traded locally for six years with no registration; rebranding would cost about $6,000. Which response best serves the owner's interests?

options.label: Rebrand at once and apologise in writing, since a national chain with more money would almost certainly win in court
Have a lawyer assess confusion risk, prior local use and rebrand cost, then reply before the deadline
Ignore the letter, since a demand letter has no legal force unless a court has issued it, and wait to be sued
Reply directly that six years of local trading gives you the name by right, and refuse to change it without advice

rubric: Prior use, confusion risk and cost trade-offs must be assessed before choosing to fight, negotiate or rebrand.
Distractors capitulate prematurely, ignore a real warning, or assert rights without advice.

items.prompt: A founder says: "We are an LLC, so I can never be personally liable for anything the business does." Which critique of this claim is soundest?

options.label: The shield protects members from tort claims but not contract debts, so members are typically liable on the company's contracts
Registration makes the LLC a separate legal person, so courts treat members as shielded from liability however they run the company
Personal liability can still arise from his own torts, personal guarantees he signs, and veil piercing if he commingles funds
The shield generally applies once an LLC has two or more members, since single-member entities usually receive no liability protection

rubric: The LLC shield is real but not absolute: own wrongdoing, guarantees and veil piercing remain.
Distractors reflect the beliefs that the shield is total, that it covers only torts, or that it needs several members.

items.prompt: A startup must demo its unpatented pricing algorithm to a prospective partner. Criteria: keep the method secret, stay enforceable, and avoid stalling the deal. Which approach is best?

options.label: Share everything first and add an NDA later, since a signed deal builds trust and secrecy then follows automatically
Sign a mutual NDA defining the confidential material and permitted use, and disclose only what the demo needs
Rely on copyright in the source code, since it prevents anyone from reusing the underlying method described in it
Mark the slides "confidential" and proceed, since a label alone creates a binding duty of non-use on the viewer

rubric: A defined NDA plus need-to-know disclosure protects trade-secret status and is enforceable.
Distractors rely on labels, on copyright (which protects expression, not methods), or on trust after disclosure.

items.prompt: A firm's contract calls a designer an "independent contractor", yet the firm sets her daily hours, supplies her laptop, bars her from other clients and directs her tasks. Which assessment is soundest?

options.label: The real working relationship decides status, so these facts point to employment and expose the firm to back-pay claims
Status turns on payment method alone, so paying her by invoice instead of payroll keeps her a contractor in law
Only the designer can ever challenge her status, so the firm carries no risk unless she personally chooses to sue
The written label decides her status, so the firm is safe as long as both parties signed the contract in good faith

rubric: Courts and agencies look at substance (control, tools, exclusivity), not the label.
Distractors treat the label, the payment method or the absence of a complaint as decisive.

items.prompt: A buyer discovers in March that a supplier delivered defective goods, but keeps accepting deliveries and paying in full until September, then tries to terminate for the March breach. How strong is its position?

options.label: Strong, because a breach gives the buyer a permanent right to terminate whenever it later decides to invoke it
Strong, because silence can never amount to affirmation of a contract unless the contract expressly says that it does
Weak, because performing on without reserving rights can be treated as affirming the contract and waiving termination
Weak, because termination is only available if the buyer first obtains a court order that confirms the breach occurred

rubric: Continuing to perform without reservation risks affirmation or waiver of the right to terminate.
Distractors assume termination rights never lapse or that a court order is always required.

items.prompt: A company commissions a logo from a freelance designer, pays the invoice, and never signs any assignment. Which judgement about ownership is most accurate in a typical common-law setting?

options.label: The company owns it because it appears on its products, since public use establishes ownership over time
The designer likely keeps copyright without a signed assignment, so the company holds at most an implied licence
Nobody owns it, because logos are not protected until they are registered as trademarks with an official office
Paying the invoice automatically transfers copyright to the company, since commissioning and paying create ownership

rubric: Copyright transfer generally requires a written assignment; payment gives at most an implied licence.
Distractors confuse payment, use or trademark registration with copyright ownership.

items.prompt: A draft contract bars a junior sales assistant from working in any industry, anywhere in the world, for five years after leaving. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Barring work in any industry goes beyond the employer's protectable business interests
Non-competes are void in every legal system, so drafting details are irrelevant to enforceability
A five-year duration likely exceeds what is needed to protect the employer's interests
A worldwide scope is broader than any legitimate interest the employer has in a junior role
A non-compete is invalid unless the employee's own lawyer countersigned it, whatever its terms

rubric: Enforceability usually depends on reasonable scope, duration and a protectable interest.
Distractors claim blanket invalidity or invent a lawyer-countersignature requirement.

items.prompt: A buyer wants a small firm's customer contracts and brand. It fears unknown pending lawsuits and unpaid tax liabilities in the firm. The seller is open to either a share sale or an asset sale. Which approach best limits inherited risk?

options.label: Buy the shares, because the company's liabilities stay with the sellers once ownership of the shares passes to the buyer
Buy the shares with an oral promise from sellers to cover surprises, which is as reliable as written warranties are
Buy the assets and assume only listed liabilities, while checking which contracts need consent to transfer
Buy the assets, since customer contracts always transfer automatically to any buyer without anyone's consent being needed

rubric: An asset purchase lets the buyer choose which liabilities to assume, though contract assignment may need consent.
Distractors assume share buyers escape liabilities, trust oral promises, or ignore consent to assignment.

items.prompt: Design a liability clause for a SaaS contract. Constraints: the supplier wants a general cap, the customer wants meaningful data-breach cover, and the law bars limiting liability for fraud or negligent death. Which clause set meets all three?

options.label: No cap anywhere, so the customer is protected on data breach and the clause cannot be challenged by the supplier later
General cap of 12 months' fees, data breach excluded entirely, and fraud limited to that same cap to keep terms uniform
General cap of 12 months' fees, higher separate cap for data breach, no limit for fraud or negligent death
One cap of 12 months' fees covering every claim, fraud and negligent death included, for the sake of simplicity and certainty

rubric: Only this set gives a general cap, a higher breach cap, and carve-outs the law requires.
Distractors breach the legal limit, drop the customer's breach cover, or abandon the supplier's cap.

items.prompt: Two founders are incorporating. They want a departing founder to keep a fair share of what they earned but not walk away with the full stake after a few months. Which design meets both aims?

options.label: Issue all founder shares fully vested at signing and rely on a verbal understanding that a leaver will hand some back
Add a non-compete for departing founders, which restricts their future work and is meant to protect the equity already granted
Grant shares under multi-year vesting with a cliff, plus a company right to buy back unvested shares on departure
Pay a departing founder a cash bonus at exit, which is intended to settle any claim to the shares already issued

rubric: Vesting with a buyback right ties equity to time served while letting leavers keep what has vested.
Distractors rely on verbal promises, unrelated restrictions, or a payment that does not alter issued shares.

items.prompt: A startup's plan for handling customers' personal data includes a privacy notice, a cookie banner and database encryption. Which addition fills the most important gap in the design?

options.label: A stronger encryption algorithm for the database, since stored-data security is the main privacy duty
An outside privacy lawyer to review each product release, since regulators expect legal sign-off on all data collection
A data inventory of personal data held and vendors receiving it, with written data-processing contracts
A consent pop-up on every page asking users to accept all processing, since consent is the basis for all data use

rubric: Knowing what data is held and where it flows, and papering vendor processing, underpins compliance.
Distractors treat technology, trademarks or headcount as substitutes for mapping data and vendor contracts.

items.prompt: Draft payment and IP terms for a custom software project. Constraints: the client pays only for working deliverables, the developer is shielded from endless change requests, and IP ownership is unambiguous. Which package fits?

options.label: Milestone payments tied to written acceptance criteria with deemed acceptance after review, written change control, and IP assignment on final payment
Full payment upfront with no acceptance criteria, change requests handled by phone as needed, and IP transferring to the client when work begins
Payment when the client is satisfied at its sole discretion, unlimited free change requests sent by email, and IP staying with the developer permanently under a licence
Payment on a fixed calendar date regardless of what is delivered, unlimited revisions at no extra charge, and IP shared equally with no defined scope of use

rubric: Acceptance criteria, change control and a defined assignment satisfy every constraint.
Distractors leave payment subjective, change uncontrolled, or ownership unclear.

items.prompt: A company wants to own inventions made by employees and contractors, but its counsel warns against overreaching clauses that courts may refuse to enforce. Which design meets both goals?

options.label: Rely on the employment relationship alone for contractors, since contractors automatically assign their inventions to clients
Use signed written assignments for employees and contractors covering work related to the business or made with company resources
Agree orally that the company owns inventions, since a spoken promise is as easy to prove as a signed document
Require every employee to assign all inventions ever made, including hobby projects on personal time unrelated to the business

rubric: A written, reasonably scoped assignment for both groups secures ownership without overreach.
Distractors overclaim, assume contractors assign automatically, or depend on oral promises.

items.prompt: A manufacturer is drafting an exclusive distribution agreement for one territory. It wants exclusivity to be earned and its brand protected. Which provisions fit these aims? Select all that apply.

options.label: Perpetual exclusivity with no performance obligations, so the distributor feels secure
A right to end or convert to non-exclusive if targets are missed
Permission for the distributor to register the brand locally in its own name
A defined territory and a statement that trademarks remain the manufacturer's property
Minimum annual purchase targets as a condition of keeping exclusivity

rubric: Targets, a consequence for missing them, and clear territory and brand ownership meet both aims.
Distractors grant unearned exclusivity or let the distributor take the brand.

items.prompt: A small company's owner is leasing a new shop. The landlord demands a personal guarantee. The owner wants to keep the lease, limit personal exposure, and keep the company as the tenant. Which proposal best meets all three?

options.label: Refuse any guarantee outright, since a landlord cannot lawfully ask for one from a company with limited liability
Sign the lease personally to speed approval, since the company's limited liability applies to personal signatures anyway
Sign for the company and offer a guarantee capped at six months' rent that ends after two years of on-time payments
Give an unlimited guarantee in return for the landlord's oral assurance that it will never be enforced against him

rubric: A capped, time-limited guarantee with the company as tenant balances the landlord's need and the owner's exposure.
Distractors expose the owner personally, misstate the law, or rely on an unenforceable oral assurance.
